paragraphs.text: Most of the world’s liquid fresh water is underground, and almost none of it is visible. Rain that does not run off or evaporate seeps between grains of sand and cracks in rock until it reaches a layer that holds it, and the store that results is measured in decades or centuries of accumulation. That timescale is the source of both the value and the trouble: an aquifer is a savings account that took a very long time to fill and can be emptied in a working lifetime.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Pumping changed the arithmetic within a generation. Before cheap engines, a well produced what a person or an animal could lift, which was a natural limit on use; a diesel pump lifts in an hour what a bucket lifts in a week. The spread of pumps transformed agriculture in dry regions, lifted tens of millions of households out of poverty and did so without anyone deciding how much water there was to lift. The technology arrived long before the measurement did.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Measurement is genuinely hard. A farmer can see a river fall and cannot see an aquifer fall, and the usual indicator — the level in a well — reflects local pumping as much as the state of the whole body. Since 2002 a pair of satellites has measured tiny changes in the pull of gravity as they pass over the Earth, and because water has mass, the loss of it shows up as a change in that pull; the resulting maps show several of the world’s largest aquifers losing water year after year. The method is coarse, cannot distinguish groundwater from snow, and is the best regional measure available.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The consequences are not only a shortage of water. As water is removed, the sediments it was holding apart compact, and the ground above them sinks; parts of several major farming valleys have dropped by more than eight metres over a century, taking roads, canals and pipelines with them. The compaction also destroys the space that held the water, so the capacity lost is permanent: even a decade of good rain cannot restore an aquifer that has closed up.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Coastal aquifers fail in a different way. Fresh water sits above salt water in a wedge whose shape depends on the pressure of the fresh water above; pump too hard and the boundary moves inland, and a well that has produced fresh water for forty years begins to produce something that kills the crop it was irrigating. Recovering such an aquifer means putting water back for as long as it took to spoil, which few places have managed and several have attempted.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Law has struggled to keep up because the resource is invisible and shared. Surface water has been governed for centuries by rules about who may take what from a river that everyone can see; groundwater in many places is still attached to the land above it, so a landowner may pump what lies beneath, and the neighbour’s well falling is not a legal injury. Where this rule has been replaced, the replacement has usually come after a crisis rather than before one, and it has taken the form of quotas, metering and a market in rights.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: What works is dull and local. Metering every well is the foundation, because a resource that is not measured cannot be limited; quotas set slightly below current use, with trading allowed between farms, cut extraction without deciding centrally which crops are worth growing. Recharge schemes, in which winter floodwater is deliberately spread on fields to soak downwards, return a useful fraction where the soil allows it. The measures that fail are the ones that skip the metering and go straight to exhortation.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The uncomfortable arithmetic is that a great deal of food is grown with water that is not being replaced, and it is exported. A tonne of grain represents roughly a thousand tonnes of water, so a country short of water can import food instead of growing it, and several have made that choice deliberately. The corresponding choice is being made accidentally by countries that export food grown on a falling water table, selling a resource they do not price at a price that does not include it.
paragraphs.label: H
